points: A general acid is written HA; in water it dissociates by donating a proton to water: HA(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ H₃O⁺(aq) + A⁻(aq), or simply HA(aq) ⇌ H⁺(aq) + A⁻(aq).
For example, ethanoic acid dissociates as CH₃COOH(aq) ⇌ CH₃COO⁻(aq) + H⁺(aq); A⁻ is the ethanoate ion.
A general base that contains hydroxide is written BOH: BOH(aq) ⇌ B⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq).
A base such as ammonia, written B, produces OH⁻ by accepting a proton from water: NH₃(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ NH₄⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq).
Here B⁺ is the ammonium ion, NH₄⁺ (BH⁺ in some books).
For a strong acid or base the dissociation goes to completion, shown by a single arrow (→); for a weak acid or base it is an equilibrium (⇌) that lies well to the left.
Step 1: Write the equilibrium: HA + H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + A⁻.
Step 2: Write Kc as products over reactants: Kc = [H₃O⁺][A⁻] ÷ ([HA][H₂O]).
Step 3: In a dilute solution [H₂O] is effectively constant (55.6 mol L⁻¹), so it is combined with Kc: Ka = Kc × [H₂O].
Result: Ka = [H₃O⁺][A⁻] ÷ [HA], or in simplified form Ka = [H⁺][A⁻] ÷ [HA]; Ka is the acid dissociation constant.
Example: for ethanoic acid, Ka = [CH₃COO⁻][H⁺] ÷ [CH₃COOH] = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ at 25 °C.
The units of Ka are mol L⁻¹ (concentration² ÷ concentration); they are often omitted.
For B + H₂O ⇌ B⁺ + OH⁻ (or BOH ⇌ B⁺ + OH⁻), the same steps give the base dissociation constant: Kb = [B⁺][OH⁻] ÷ [B] (or [B⁺][OH⁻] ÷ [BOH]).
[H₂O] is again effectively constant and is absorbed into Kb.
Example: for ammonia, Kb = [NH₄⁺][OH⁻] ÷ [NH₃] = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ at 25 °C.

notes.h: What Ka and Kb tell you (Higher Level only)
points: Ka measures the strength of an acid, its tendency to donate a proton: the larger Ka, the further the equilibrium lies to the right and the stronger the acid.
Likewise, the larger Kb, the stronger the base.
Weak acids have small Ka values (much less than 1): methanoic acid 1.8 × 10⁻⁴, benzoic acid 6.3 × 10⁻⁵, ethanoic acid 1.8 × 10⁻⁵, propanoic acid 1.3 × 10⁻⁵ (strongest to weakest).
Strong acids (HCl, HNO₃, H₂SO₄) and strong bases (NaOH, KOH) dissociate essentially completely, so their Ka or Kb values are very large and the expressions are not used.
Ka and Kb are used for weak acids and bases.
Like all equilibrium constants, Ka and Kb are constant at a given temperature and do not change with concentration; values are quoted at 25 °C.
Step 1: Start with c mol L⁻¹ of a weak acid HA, of which x mol L⁻¹ dissociates. At equilibrium [HA] = c − x, [H⁺] = x and [A⁻] = x.
Step 2: Ka = x × x ÷ (c − x) = x² ÷ (c − x).
Step 3: A weak acid dissociates so little that x is tiny compared with c, so c − x ≈ c and Ka = x² ÷ c.
Step 4: x² = Ka × c, so [H⁺] = √(Ka × c).
The same steps for a weak base give [OH⁻] = √(Kb × c); worked uses of both formulas are in “pH calculations”.

keyTerms.definition: The equilibrium constant for a weak acid dissociating in water, Ka = [H⁺][A⁻] ÷ [HA].
The equilibrium constant for a weak base reacting with water, Kb = [B⁺][OH⁻] ÷ [B].
An acid that dissociates only partly in water, so its dissociation is an equilibrium that lies to the left.
A base that accepts a proton from water only partly, forming a small amount of OH⁻.
The splitting of a molecule into ions when it dissolves in water.
The ion CH₃COO⁻ formed when ethanoic acid dissociates.
The ion NH₄⁺ formed when ammonia accepts a proton from water.

questions.prompt: Write equations for the dissociation in water of (i) a weak acid HA, (ii) ammonia, and state the difference between the dissociation of a strong acid and a weak acid.
questions.model: (i) HA(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ H₃O⁺(aq) + A⁻(aq), or HA(aq) ⇌ H⁺(aq) + A⁻(aq). (ii) NH₃(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ NH₄⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq). A strong acid dissociates completely, shown by a single arrow (→), whereas a weak acid dissociates only partly, as an equilibrium (⇌) that lies well to the left.

questions.prompt: Write the expression for the acid dissociation constant, Ka, of ethanoic acid. Explain why [H₂O] does not appear in it, and what a small Ka value tells you about the acid.
questions.model: Ka = [CH₃COO⁻][H⁺] ÷ [CH₃COOH], equivalently [H₃O⁺][CH₃COO⁻] ÷ [CH₃COOH]. Water is the solvent and is present in such large excess that its concentration, 55.6 mol L⁻¹, is effectively constant; it is combined with Kc to give Ka, so [H₂O] does not appear in the expression. Ka for ethanoic acid is 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ at 25 °C. A small Ka means the equilibrium lies well to the left, so only a small proportion of the acid is dissociated and the acid is weak.

questions.prompt: Starting from the Ka expression, show that the hydrogen ion concentration of a weak acid of concentration c is approximately √(Ka × c), stating the assumption made.
questions.model: Let x mol L⁻¹ of a weak acid HA of concentration c mol L⁻¹ dissociate. At equilibrium [HA] = c − x, [H⁺] = x and [A⁻] = x. Then Ka = x × x ÷ (c − x) = x² ÷ (c − x). Assumption: the acid dissociates so little that x is tiny compared with c, so c − x ≈ c. Then Ka = x² ÷ c, so x² = Ka × c and [H⁺] = x = √(Ka × c).
